newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Multinationals key to Ireland's strong growth-OECD.
newsitem.headline: Multinationals key to Ireland's strong growth-OECD.

text.p: Direct investment by overseas multinational companies has been central to Ireland's outstanding growth levels, with the economy expanding by 22 percent in the last three years, the OECD said.

Ireland's growth rate was more than three times that of the European Union and North America, and on par with countries in the Pacific region of the OECD such as Korea and New Zealand, the Paris-based research body said in a survey, part of a series entitled Economic Surveys 1996/7.
The report was due for release on Wednesday but sections of it were published earlyl by local media.
It said that while macroeconomic policies helped, three favourable elements, in particular, were associated with Ireland's economic growth.

Direct investment by overseas multinational companies; an expanding well-qualified labour force; and a social consensus on pay policy that has left management free to concentrate on improving efficiency, the OECD said.
The number of foreign firms, led by American companies, investing in Ireland has risen by over 50 percent during the last 10 years, it said.

"According to U.S. data, the total stock of investment by American firms in the Irish manufacturing sector rose by 45 percent to $6.9 billion, or 12 percent of Ireland's GNP, between 1992-1995," the report said.
Most foreign investment has been in areas like computers, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals and soft drink concentrates.

The OECD report said Irish government policy had played a key role in attracting foreign investment. It lauded the government's sound fiscal and monetary management, supported by an effective incomes policy which allowed continued wage moderation.

The introduction of a special 10 percent corporate tax rate, which applies to the entire manufacturing sector until end-2010 was also key. So was the establishment of the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) in 1987 as a base for international banking, insurance, leading and fund management.
The special 10 percent tax rate was extended to companies operating in the IFSC in 1990 until end-2005.

While the tax regime has been an important factor in drawing foreign companies to Ireland, the availability of low-cost, well-qualified labour, stemming from the government's education and training policies, has also been essential, the OECD said.

It said the combination of these various factors has made manufacturing investment profitable. For example, in 1995 U.S. companies earned a post-tax rate of return of 23 percent on capital, up to five times higher than that of U.S. companies elsewhere in Europe, it said.
